extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians writing research papers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, opinionated guidelines for composing clear, readable mathematical research papers (title/abstract/introduction/structure/notation/references/LaTeX/after-publication). Focuses on clarity for typical readers and arXiv-era dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (the Golden Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity is "absolutely paramount." It means clarity in idea, not just phrasing; you must think of the reader and how they will read your paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being clear is hard and slow; clarity benefits all readers (grad students, skimmers, juniors). Journals/copy editors do not fix clarity. "For the sake of clarity, ignore all rules." Emphasise making the idea and exposition accessible rather than obeying formal stylistic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with existing literature and writing guides
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by studying other mathematicians' writing (Halmos, Higham, Knuth, Krantz, Berndt, Goldreich, S.P. Jones, Tao's blog) and a non‑fiction writing guide (Zinsser).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt general writing advice to mathematics; learning from exemplars speeds the writing process and improves clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph length and whitespace
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep paragraphs short; two‑three sentence 'newspaper' paragraphs are fine; leave air around prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short paragraphs help modern readers who skim. Avoid the opposite extreme of overly terse, verbless 'midget' paragraphs that sacrifice coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for clarity rather than perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer *clear* to *perfect* writing because modern readers skim and may only read introductions or arXiv summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't delay publication seeking flawless prose; ensure the central ideas are plainly communicated. Update versions later if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall structure (Matryoshka principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organise the paper as nested summaries: Title -> Abstract -> Introduction -> Main part -> Final remarks -> References; give a brief summary first, then progressively longer ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hook the reader early with short then longer summaries; reserve full technical facts for later sections after the reader is engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title: content-focused and informative
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles should not be too long, too short, vague, or generic; the title is the first approximation of the paper's contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tricks like naming your objects (e.g., 'Munro permutations') so the title can reference them. Emphasise content (e.g., 'Short proof that all tennis balls are white' beats vague alternatives). For surveys, explicitly signal 'A survey on...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: dry facts and key results first
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should be like a short MathSciNet summary: state key results first, be dry, avoid precise technical statements and excessive detail or other-work connections unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length rule of thumb: about 0.3–0.5 lines per page. Keep abstracts concise and factual; do not include technicalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of Contents: include only for very long papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Skip a table of contents unless the paper exceeds about 60 pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern PDF readers provide navigation; only lengthy manuscripts benefit substantially from a TOC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: the most important section
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction is likely the only part read by most readers; it should set up the problem, state main results (first theorem on page 1 or 2), and outline the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a senior coauthor or colleague review it. Draft it early and rewrite after finishing the body; let it 'stew' with feedback for a week. Do not include technical definitions or big figures—refer to their sections. Explain only directly‑relevant history; the last paragraph should outline the structure of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreword for long intros; single literary opening paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: For long introductions, include a non‑technical 'Foreword' subsection to provide big‑picture, philosophical, or literary context; even short papers can benefit from one memorable opening paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the place for material that might be quoted in other papers; use it to present the 'shining' nontechnical view of your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Remarks: expanded endnotes and ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Use final remarks as an endnotes/footnotes section with short untitled subsections (one paragraph to one page each), ordered by decreasing importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include history first, then future directions, speculative conjectures, and others' conjectures. Use this section as a 'dump' while writing and cross‑reference it (e.g., 'for more on this, see §6.1').

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgements: be specific and generous
rubrics_metrics.description: Give lavish acknowledgements, ordering people by increasing importance and listing names alphabetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank everyone who discussed the work; single out specific contributors with explanations. Obtain email permission before including private information. End the acknowledgements with institutions and funding agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation phrasing and reliability (twelve citation styles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wording used to cite prior work conveys reliability and the author's relationship to the cited result; there is a hierarchy of phrasing from definitive ('Roth proved ... in [Roth]') to uncertain ('Roth claims to have proved ... in [Roth]').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise, reliable phrasing when possible. Avoid ambiguous or hearsay phrasing (personal communications, unverifiable claims) except with clear caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to cite a list of papers (avoid 'see [2-19]')
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't lump many works under a single citation range like 'see [2-19]'; instead, walk through the literature individually, listing the most important works first and briefly describing each contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice serves readers and gives proper credit to authors; it improves clarity in the introduction and literature discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to place citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the most relevant references in the Introduction; other related work belongs in Final Remarks. In the main technical part, include references only for precise borrowed lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cluttering proofs with literature discussion; reserve broader context and survey‑like citations for intro/final remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming references: use stable locators
rubrics_metrics.description: Form references using section/subsection numbering (e.g., '[A, §3.1]') because arXiv pagination may change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide findable pointers that remain valid across versions and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference style and pragmatics
rubrics_metrics.description: Make references concise but findable; prefer alphanumeric labels for long papers; for many authors use shorthand (e.g., '[A+13]'); include arXiv numbers or links for unpublished papers; avoid BibTeX unless you are advanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not emulate excessive bibliographic perfectionism; prefer pragmatic, readable citations. For unpublished work, provide arXiv identifiers for discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry in notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Skip overly pedantic distinctions in notation that distract from the idea (example: avoid nitpicking Q⊂R issues), and 'just draw a picture and get on with your math.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor accessibility over formalistic obsessing; use pictures and intuition where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downshift style for broad readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust your style for a heterogeneous audience that includes non‑native English speakers and skimmers: be repetitive, use the present indefinite tense mostly, prefer short sentences, and maintain consistent terminology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use commas for structural clarity (not pauses); avoid semicolons (they imply vague logical connection); avoid long dashes without spaces; use Standard American spelling; once a term is defined, do not vary it (e.g., if you introduce 'nice graph', don't switch to 'niceness of graphs').

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX macros and consistent notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Create many LaTeX macros (e.g., '\\al' for '\\alpha') and use the same macros across papers to ensure consistency; choose mnemonic letters for categories (f,g,φ,ϕ,ζ,ξ,η,ρ for functions; a–e for constants; x,y,z for variables; i,j,k,ℓ,m,n for integers; p,q,r,s,t,u,v for other things).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letters that look alike (Ξ, ι, ϖ, ȷ, ϰ vs κ vs k). Prefer specific glyphs (use ∅ not another symbol for empty set; use ℓ not l; use ε vs ϵ consistently). Insert placeholder macros while experimenting with notation; finalize fonts at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not blindly trust LaTeX typesetting
rubrics_metrics.description: LaTeX spacing and typesetting can introduce ambiguity (e.g., adjacent math symbols can be unreadable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually insert spacing (such as '\\,') to disambiguate expressions; check rendered output carefully for ambiguous symbol adjacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures (clarity and usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures deserve careful attention (section continued in remaining pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although detailed figure guidance continues beyond the fetched excerpt, treat figures as tools to clarify ideas; avoid oversized figures in the introduction and prefer references to figure sections when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication maintenance and promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: You are never really done: keep updating the arXiv version, advertise and popularise your work, and consider rewriting or republishing if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the paper's clarity and correctness over time; use arXiv updates and outreach to maximise impact.
